drapeaux.note: Fragments of Article I, Section 2 (“three fifths of all other Persons”) and the Fourteenth Amendment, Section 2 (“the whole number of persons in each State”) use the official English wording of the Constitution; not re-checked against a live page in this pass.

Pierce Butler's line, quoted in French as « l'argent est le pouvoir », is rendered “money is power” (Madison's notes, June 11, 1787, likely “money was power”); the exact English wording was not confirmed against the Avalon/Madison text.

titre: The Three-Fifths Clause: The South Wanted to Count Enslaved People in Full
accroche: It is said that the 1787 Constitution reduces an enslaved person to three fifths of a person. In Philadelphia, the South was demanding a higher figure.
contenu_vulgarise:
## What the Text Says

Article I, Section 2, of the 1787 U.S. Constitution governs the apportionment of representatives and direct taxes among the states. The number of inhabitants is calculated by adding to the number of free persons, including those bound to service for a term of years, and excluding Indians not taxed, “three fifths of all other Persons.” The clause does not use the word “slave”: it speaks of “all other Persons.” It is a counting rule, for dividing seats and a tax burden.

## Who Wanted What

The formula was not born in Philadelphia. On April 18, 1783, the Congress of the Confederation had proposed apportioning the states' contributions by population rather than by land value, counting three fifths of enslaved people. The amendment fails: unanimity is lacking, with New York and New Hampshire opposed.

On June 11, 1787, at the Convention, James Wilson, seconded by Charles Pinckney of South Carolina, proposes adopting this ratio for representation. The Southern delegates defend the weight of wealth. South Carolinian Pierce Butler asserts that “money is power.” Elbridge Gerry of Massachusetts replies by asking why enslaved people, who are property in the South, should count for representation when the North's cattle do not. The proposal passes, nine states to two.

On July 12, the debate returns. Charles Pinckney proposes counting Black people equally with white people for representation. The motion fails: only South Carolina and Georgia vote in favor. The three-fifths figure is therefore the result of a bargain in which the South asked for more and the North for less, down to zero for some.

## Counting Without Recognizing

The common misreading is to take this clause as an assessment of the worth of a human being. It measures nothing of the kind: it is a rule for dividing power, which the delegates defended or fought for what it earned their state. Gerry's paradox stands intact: the same people are goods when it comes to their rights and inhabitants when it comes to their owners' seats.

The Thirteenth Amendment (1865) abolishes slavery and strips the clause of almost all its purpose. Section 2 of the Fourteenth Amendment (1868) replaces it: it counts “the whole number of persons in each State,” excluding Indians not taxed.

repere.texte: On July 12, 1787, at the Philadelphia Convention, Charles Pinckney's motion to count Black people equally with white people for representation fails: only South Carolina and Georgia vote in favor.
repere.source: James Madison, Notes of Debates in the Federal Convention, session of July 12, 1787 (Avalon Project, Yale Law School)

carte.punch: In Philadelphia, the South wanted to count enslaved people in full. The North, not at all.
carte.idee: The three-fifths clause (1787) does not say an enslaved person is worth less than a man: it sets the number of seats and taxes. On July 12, 1787, the motion to count Black people equally with white people is rejected, with only two states supporting it.

quiz.question: What position did the Southern delegates hold on counting enslaved people during the 1787 debates?
choix: They asked that they not be counted at all, to reduce their states' share of taxes
They wanted to count them in full for representation, which increased their weight
They accepted three fifths from the start and proposed no other fraction
They wanted a count specific to each state, set by Congress every year
quiz.explication: On July 12, 1787, Pinckney proposes counting Black people equally with white people for representation, and the motion fails. So it was not the South that wanted a low figure for representation, and the fraction was not accepted at the outset: the North asked for less, the South for more.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Where does the proposal to count three fifths of enslaved people, taken up at the 1787 Convention, come from?
choix: A proposal of the Congress of the Confederation, on April 18, 1783
An English bill of 1776 on colonial taxation
A proposal by George Washington presented in 1776
An agreement signed between Virginia and Massachusetts in 1781
quiz_supplementaire.explication: On April 18, 1783, the Congress of the Confederation had proposed apportioning the states' contributions by population, counting three fifths of enslaved people.

quiz_supplementaire.question: How does Elbridge Gerry respond to Pierce Butler during the debate of June 11, 1787?
choix: He proposes counting enslaved people on par with free persons
He demands the immediate abolition of slavery in all states
He asks why enslaved people, property in the South, should count for representation
He proposes removing all representation from states that practice slavery
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Gerry asks why enslaved people, who are property in the South, should count for representation when the North's cattle do not.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What did Section 2 of the Fourteenth Amendment, adopted in 1868, change compared with the three-fifths clause?
choix: It raised the fraction to four fifths of the same persons
It abolished any rule for apportioning representatives in Congress
It transferred the calculation of representation to the U.S. Senate
It now counts the whole number of persons in each State
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Section 2 of the Fourteenth Amendment counts the whole number of persons in each State, excluding Indians not taxed, and ends the three-fifths fraction.
